quote_item6: Low-quality/Misinformation Sources (LQMS) We identify the set of low-quality/questionable sources in two ways. First, we aggregate information using a list curated by NewsGuard [42]. Since the COVID-19 outbreak, they have kept a separate list of websites identified as propagating misinformation specifically related to the virus. Second, we rely on lists of low-quality and fake news producers aggregated by various scholars and fact-checking organizations [11]. ... In total, our list contains 1249 low quality sources.

quote_item6: We follow best practices (Guess, Nyhan and Reifler 2020, Grinberg et al. 2019, Lazer et al. 2018) and operationalize “sharing of fake news sources” as when panel members tweet or retweet URLs to external web domains known to publish factually incorrect news. To this end, we cross-referenced all tweeted URLs against a list of 608 fake news sources, constructed by journalists and scholars.
quote_item10: Of the 2.7 million tweets in our data, only 85,344 (≈ 3%) contain links to national news websites, fake or real. Of the tweeted news links, 3,269 (≈ 4%) come from websites with a history of publishing fake news.
notes: Osmundsen et al., YouGov US Twitter panel (N=2,337) linked to full public tweet traces (2,709,052 tweets/retweets). Item1/2 LOW: a real audience (US Twitter users), benchmarked against Pew's Twitter population on race, gender, income, education and age. Item3 LOW: complete behavioural trace of every consenting panelist. Item4 HIGH: severe and self-acknowledged attrition - 27,000+ invited, 8,741 completed, 2,337 linkable; 'Because of high and non-random attrition, our sample is unlikely to perfectly reflect any well-defined population.' Item10 LOW: both the news-link denominator and the whole-diet denominator (2.7M tweets) are reported, the concentration figure uses all fake links, and the reach figure uses the full panel; nothing here is selected on the outcome. The list has 674 low-credibility domains.

Item1/2 HIGH: keyword-defined topical corpora ('coronavirus', 'COVID', 'sars'); on the Facebook side the frame is CrowdTangle coverage, which the authors warn 'might bias the dataset in ways that are hard to gauge ... requests from researchers interested in monitoring low-credibility pages and groups might lead to over-representation of such content'. Item3 HIGH on balance: the Twitter arm is a genuine 10% random Decahose sample (would be LOW alone), but the Facebook arm - half of the headline comparison - is a non-random convenience corpus of public pages/groups. Item4/5 NA: content analysis; note there is no leaf-user information on Facebook at all. Item6 LOW: MBFC-derived 674-domain list, source-level. Item8 HIGH: the two arms use structurally different instruments and metrics (retweets vs reshares, 10% sample vs page-level census; reshare:post ratio 68:1 against retweet:tweet 2.7:1) yet the 32% vs 21% contrast is read as a like-for-like difference. Item9 LOW: 10 months, stated. Item10 HIGH: 'ratio of low-credibility information' is low-credibility over (low- + high-credibility) links - an explicitly benchmarked, curated denominator that excludes everything else people saw; the concentration estimates (40%/70% verified-account share) likewise use low-credibility shares as their base.

quote_item6: Posts were considered harmful if they recommended pharmacologic or nonpharmacologic therapies (eg, stem cell transplant, specific dietary modifications) not recommended by current IPF guidelines (see Table S3 in Multimedia Appendix 1 for examples of nonrecommended therapies).
quote_item10: Only 5% of the posts contained potentially harmful information, but 35% of all groups or pages contained such posts.
notes: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Facebook groups and pages, 523 posts. Item1/2 HIGH: the universe is whatever Facebook's own search returned for 'IPF' and 'idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis' on one day (126 groups + 191 pages screened to 12 + 27); a disease-community frame, not an audience or a public. Item3 LOW: eligible groups/pages were taken as a census and every 10th post was sampled systematically. Item4/5 NA: content analysis. Item6 HIGH: this is the clearest CONTENT-vs-QUALITY substitution in the shard - 'harmful' is defined as recommending therapies not endorsed by clinical guidelines, i.e. guideline non-adherence standing in for falsity; the study never asks whether a post is false. Item7 LOW: duplicate independent coding by two authors against 30 prespecified guideline-supported content items, unweighted kappa with a 0.70 acceptability threshold and third-author arbitration below it (the kappa values themselves are not printed in the main text). Item9 HIGH: 'Cross-sectional analysis was performed on a single date' - there is no prevalence period at all; posts of arbitrary and unreported age are pooled into a single percentage. Item10 HIGH: 5% of 523 posts drawn from IPF-focused groups and pages; the alternative denominator offered (35% of groups or pages) shifts the unit again without defining an audience.
